DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26

The report's recommendation rests on a causal claim the data can't support, and its headline overall figure is wrong. I'd treat it as not ready for the Board in its current form.

## 1. Arithmetic error: overall uptake is not 66%
Table 1 does not add up. The vaccinated total of 13,772 divided by 22,080 eligible pupils gives **62.4%**, not 66.0%. The row figures are consistent with each other (6,384/9,120 = 70.0%, 7,388/12,960 = 57.0%), and a weighted average of the two groups also gives about 62.4%.

- The claim that Eastvale is "above the national ambition of 65% for the first time" is false on the report's own numbers. Eastvale is about 2.6 points **below** the ambition.
- The author's "building on success" framing depends on this error.
- The 66% may be the consent-rate-adjacent figure or a typo (consent return overall is 67.1%). It needs checking at source.

## 2. The 13-point gap is not a causal effect
Schools opted in. This was not randomised, and the report itself shows the groups differ in ways that plausibly drive uptake:
- **Full-time school nurse:** 29 of 38 reminder schools, against 11 of 54 others.
- **Geography and affluence:** reminder schools are disproportionately in the affluent west. The lowest-uptake schools are in the east.
- **Contactability:** 93% of families in reminder schools have a valid mobile number, against 61% elsewhere.

Schools that opt in are also likely to be more organised and engaged, which would raise uptake regardless of texts. The report has no baseline, such as 2024-25 uptake by school, so it cannot show whether reminder schools were already ahead. The statements that reminders "raise uptake by around 13 points" and are "the clearest evidence" are unsupported. The 13 points is an upper bound on the effect at best. A difference-in-differences against prior years, or an adjusted or stratified comparison (for example, nurse versus no nurse), would be the minimum.

## 3. The effect won't transfer to the schools being targeted
Section 4 undermines Section 6.
- In the 54 non-reminder schools, **39% of families have no usable mobile number**, so reminders can't reach them.
- These schools also have more families who speak another language at home, higher household mobility, and paper forms returned incomplete. Texts with an English-language link to an online portal address none of these barriers.
- The assumption that uptake will rise "from 57% to around 70%" and bring "every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" assumes the full effect transfers to the hardest-to-reach population. That is the least likely outcome.
- Uptake in non-reminder schools ranges from 38% to 79%. The report gives no spread for reminder schools, so an average effect is a poor guide for individual schools.

## 4. Unsupported comparative claim
"More than any other intervention we have tried" is not backed by any comparison. The only other intervention mentioned, mop-up sessions, is said to add 3-6 points, and it was offered in only 14 schools. No cost per additional child vaccinated is given for either. "By far the cheapest route" is therefore asserted rather than shown.

## 5. The cost analysis is less cautious than described
- The send cost is arithmetically fine (4,990 × 3 × £0.08 ≈ £1,198), and the total of about £4,250 is under £5,000.
- It is not conservative in the ways that matter. It excludes the cost of **collecting or correcting missing mobile numbers** for about 39% of families, any translation or accessible-format materials, and staff time for the extra children who would need to be vaccinated. A one-off £2,500 data-linking charge won't fix missing data.
- Because 39% of families can't be texted, the sending cost is somewhat overstated, but the real constraint is reach, not price.
- Low cost does not show cost-effectiveness. The cost per additional vaccinated child can't be calculated without a credible effect estimate.

## 6. Framing and process concerns
- The author describes this as a "clean" comparison and says they "looked hard for reasons not to scale" and found none. The report contains several such reasons (points 2 and 3), which suggests confirmation bias.
- "Consent is the bottleneck" is reasonable (about 92-93% of consented children were vaccinated in both groups). However, "texts act directly on consent" treats non-return as forgetfulness. For the lowest-uptake schools, the barriers appear to be language, incomplete forms and missing contact details.
- **Equity risk:** a universal roll-out of a channel that reaches affluent, contactable families best could widen the gap between east and west.

## Recommendations
1. Correct the overall uptake figure (about 62.4%) and remove the claim of exceeding the 65% ambition.
2. Reframe the finding as an association, and add baseline or prior-year data and adjusted or stratified analysis (nurse and ward).
3. Replace the 70% projection with a range that reflects reduced reach and effect in eastern schools.
4. Plan to improve mobile-number coverage and multilingual and assisted consent routes alongside reminders.
5. Compare reminders against mop-up sessions on cost per additional child vaccinated.
6. Consider a staged or randomised roll-out in the 54 non-reminder schools in 2026-27, which would give a real effect estimate while still extending the service.
